Participants identify their sandbox, find memory pressure, locate a file filling the disk, and clean up background processes. items.title: Evals in AI: A Deep Dive — Tejas Kumar, IBM
items.content_snippet: A customer support answer passes a test because it contains the word “cannot,” even though it approves a return outside the store's policy. Tejas Kumar builds that failure live to show where ordinary assertions and fuzzy matching stop being useful. The example grows into an LLM judge, then a dataset of customer scenarios, agent responses, and human verdicts. Along the way, the judge starts favoring an answer generated by its own model family. items.title: Your AI Agent Is Confidently Wrong About Production — Willem Pienaar, Cleric

items.title: Agent Memory Is Solved. Agent Learning Isn't. — Karthik Ranganathan, Yugabyte
items.content_snippet: One agent can remember. A team of agents still can't learn together. Karthik Ranganathan, co-founder and co-CEO of Yugabyte, explains why per-agent memory is a solved problem but shared learning across agents isn't. When one agent hands work to another, it passes on the output but loses the reasoning, the dead ends and the context, so the next agent burns tokens re-deriving it all. items.title: Agents That Write Their Own Tools at Runtime — Sandhya Subramani, AWS
items.content_snippet: This agent starts with zero tools. Ask it for something it can't do, and it writes the tool and uses it without restarting. Sandhya Subramani, senior developer advocate for GenAI at AWS, demos meta-tooling with the open-source Strands Agents SDK. That means agents that write, load and use their own tools at runtime, and even spin up their own sub-agents. items.title: AI Coding Agents Are Breaking Big Codebases — Dan Adler, Sourcegraph
items.content_snippet: Claude Code can make the change. But what if you have 90,000 repositories to make it in? Dan Adler, CEO of Sourcegraph, makes the case for the people who own the huge, decades-old codebases that run banks, cars and airlines. Coding agents are producing a tidal wave of code, and those codebases are starting to decay through duplicated code, drifting standards, brittle dependencies and new vulnerabilities. items.title: Keyword Search Is Dying. Is Your Catalog Ready for AI Agents? — PayPal
items.content_snippet: Shoppers are moving from typing keywords to describing what they need, and agents are doing the searching. Nixon Dinh, director of product for agentic commerce at PayPal, explains how shopping is moving from the search era to the intent era and then the delegation era, and why product catalogs built for keyword SEO aren't ready for AI agents. items.title: The Human Is an Async API — Melanie Warrick, Temporal
items.content_snippet: Humans don't respond in 200 milliseconds. Your agent shouldn't fall over waiting for one. Melanie Warrick from developer relations at Temporal shows how to build human-in-the-loop agents that don't block or lose state.
